w: Nearly 190,000 square feet of gallery space and 22,000 works, Old Masters next to Latin American modernism next to contemporary prints, make this one of the largest university art museums in the country. The Washington Post ranked it among the nation's best college museums in 2024.
s: One of America's biggest university art museums
_facts: 189,340 square feet devoted to galleries, storage and programs
permanent collection of more than 22,000 works spanning modern, Latin American, Old Master and print collections
ranked by the Washington Post in 2024 as one of the five best college art museums in the US

w: Austin knew it as Pecan Street before the grid renamed it, and by the 1970s it had become the city's live-music engine, Victorian storefronts from the 1880s repurposed into bars, clubs and stages. The nine-block historic core made the National Register in 1975 and never stopped playing.
s: Pecan Street's second life as a music strip
_facts: formerly named Pecan Street
nine-block Sixth Street Historic District listed on the NRHP December 30, 1975
major entertainment district of bars, clubs and live music venues since the 1970s

w: Tourists have climbed it for the view since the 1850s, and the view hasn't needed an upgrade since, Austin, Lake Austin and the hill country laid out below. It picked up a Texas Historic Landmark marker in 1969 and a National Register listing in 2015, long after the crowds arrived.
s: A hilltop view Austin has climbed to since the 1850s
_facts: also known as Covert Park, a vista point alongside Lake Austin on the Colorado River
popular tourist destination since the 1850s
designated a Recorded Texas Historic Landmark in 1969, listed on the NRHP in 2015

w: Thirty-six million manuscripts, a million rare books, five million photographs, a research archive so vast it renamed itself from the Humanities Research Center in 1983 just to sound less modest. In one recent academic year alone, its reading room fed nearly 150 published books.
s: Thirty-six million manuscripts under one roof
_facts: holds 36 million literary manuscripts, one million rare books and five million photographs
known as the Humanities Research Center until 1983
hosted nearly 6,000 research visits in 2015-16, resulting in over 145 books

w: Two earlier dams on this exact stretch of the Colorado River were destroyed by floods before this one finally held, funded by the Public Works Administration and named for a sitting Austin mayor. It's been holding back Lake Austin since 1940, third time lucky.
s: The third dam to try this stretch of river
_facts: built by the City of Austin with Public Works Administration funds for flood control and hydroelectric power
named after Robert Thomas Miller, a former mayor of Austin, and forms Lake Austin
began operating in 1940 at the site of two earlier dams both destroyed by floods

n: Ann W. Richards Congress Avenue Bridge
w: Every spring, pregnant bats move into the underside of this concrete arch bridge and turn it into the world's largest urban bat maternity colony, males aren't even allowed back until the pups are born. Renamed for Governor Ann Richards in 2006, it's been a nursery far longer than a namesake.
s: A bridge that doubles as a bat maternity ward
_facts: home to the world's largest urban bat colony, a maternity colony where females raise pups from mid-summer to fall
males are absent from the colony until after the pups are born
renamed in 2006 for Governor Ann W. Richards, previously the Congress Avenue Bridge

w: Andrew Jackson Zilker gave the city 350 acres in 1917, and Depression-era crews turned it into a park by the 1930s, now the anchor for the hike-and-bike trail around Lady Bird Lake and the site every October where Austin City Limits takes over the grass. Listed on the National Register since 1997.
s: The 350 acres one man gave the city in 1917
_facts: over 350 acres donated by Andrew Jackson Zilker in 1917, developed into a park in the 1930s
hosts the Austin City Limits Music Festival and the Zilker Park Kite Festival
listed on the NRHP in 1997

w: A cattleman named Jesse Driskill spent his entire fortune building 'the finest hotel south of St. Louis' in 1886, and it's been checking guests in ever since, Austin's oldest continuously operating hotel, now run by Hyatt. It made the National Register in 1969.
s: A cattleman's fortune, spent on one hotel
_facts: Romanesque-style hotel completed in 1886, the oldest operating hotel in Austin
built by cattleman Col. Jesse Driskill, aiming for 'the finest hotel south of St. Louis'
listed on the NRHP November 25, 1969, operated by Hyatt since 2013

w: Austin's contemporary-art anchor started life as the Austin Museum of Art before folding itself into a two-site operation with its own art school. Locals just call it 'The Contemporary,' shorthand for whatever's newest and strangest in Texas art right now.
s: Austin's contemporary-art museum, under a new name
_facts: originally known as the Austin Museum of Art
Austin's primary contemporary art museum, with two locations and an art school
reflects contemporary art through exhibitions, commissions, education and its collection

w: Thomas McKinney ran cattle and racehorses on this land through the mid-1800s, long before the state turned it into a park in 1976 around the twin falls where Onion Creek tumbles over limestone. The old El Camino Real de los Tejas trail still cuts straight through it.
s: A rancher's land, now a park with twin falls
_facts: 744.4-acre state park at the confluence of Onion Creek and Williamson Creek, opened April 15, 1976
named after Thomas F. McKinney, a 19th-century businessman, racehorse breeder and rancher who owned the land
features scenic upper and lower falls on Onion Creek, on the El Camino Real de los Tejas National Historic Trail
